title: Systematic Thinking, BlackRock Style - Top Traders Unplugged - Ep.151

meta.source: Macro Transcripts/Systematic Thinking, BlackRock Style - Top Traders Unplugged - Ep.151.docx

speakers: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host, Top Traders Unplugged; caption spelling 'Neils Castro Larson')
summary: BlackRock Systematic's Jeff Rosenberg on the post-Covid inflation regime, weaker stock-bond diversification and the move toward liquid alternatives. Describes breadth-based trend ETFs, the defensive-alpha equity long/short built on a credit lens, and ETF wrapper constraints. Hosts worry that low-fee narrow trend ETFs hide breadth compromises.

coverage.note: intro, sponsor and compliance read, host introduces guest
guest background; macro: post-Covid inflation, stock-bond correlation
divine coincidence, persistent not resurgent inflation, Fed credibility
term premium, wages, affordability, price adjustment; fixed income as income
history of fixed income and 60/40; diversifiers; debt and financial repression
financial repression modelling; systematic definitions start
meaning of systematic, return-source separation, AI
why big managers launch trend, engineering for outcomes
trend vs momentum/factors; 2025 timing of ISMF
2025 reversals; law of active management; breadth in ETFs
cocoa 2024 and basket selection; no timing; defensive alpha intro
defensive alpha, convex profiles, combining strategies
multi-strat mix, implementation alpha, market impact
leverage constraints, contract choice, CalPERS total portfolio
ETF fee and breadth concerns, manager selection, outro
nothing actionable: outro and subscribe read

completeness_estimate: 0.79 - the first reader captured the main macro, systematic-framework, ETF and defensive-alpha ideas (64 claims) but skipped host/co-host points (unstable inflation, dual mandate, ETF fee economics, drawdown types), allocation-size reasoning and the AI/differentiation remarks

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: the precoid environment was one of too little inflation and the postcoid environment is an environment of too much inflation
claims.claim: The post-Covid shift from too little to too much (but gradually falling) inflation is a structural regime change that alters the structure of strategies and portfolios.
claims.conditions: Regime change from pre-Covid disinflation to post-Covid persistent inflation
claims.testable: partly: regime can be dated, effect on strategies testable by sub-period

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: the relationship between risky assets and safe assets. stock bond correlation
claims.claim: Higher inflation challenges the stock-bond correlation, the key construct for portfolio construction, so bond diversification is less reliable.
claims.direction: stock-bond correlation rises (positive)
claims.testable: yes: rolling stock-bond correlation vs inflation level

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: divine coincidence of monetary policy exists when you have too little inflation
claims.claim: With too little inflation the Fed has no conflict between its mandates (easing helps both), which made bonds powerful diversifiers; with too much inflation there is no riskless policy path and that diversification weakens.
claims.direction: bonds diversify equities when inflation is low and easing is costless; not when inflation is above target
claims.conditions: Inflation near or below target vs persistently above target
claims.testable: yes: bond hedge efficacy conditional on inflation regime

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: resurgent inflation really means first and foremost a lack of the continual collapse of inflation down to the 2% target
claims.claim: The practical inflation risk is persistent above-target inflation (about 3%) rather than a return of Covid-level inflation.
claims.testable: partly: inflation persistence can be measured

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: So, there's a credibility problem.
claims.claim: If the Fed tolerates about 3% inflation while saying its target is 2%, credibility suffers and investors may not be compensated for that inflation in long bonds (term premium).
claims.direction: higher term premium needed on long bonds
claims.testable: partly: term premium is a model estimate

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: that's a big debate around term premium and the value of uh the hedging efficacy of back-end yields versus front-end yields
claims.claim: Inflation uncertainty raises term premium and reduces the hedging efficacy of long-end versus front-end yields.
claims.indicator: term premium, long-end vs front-end yields
claims.direction: long-end yields less effective hedge; term premium up
claims.testable: yes: hedge beta by maturity over time

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: So, you got to kind of watch this kind of petering out of the decline in the wage inflation figures
claims.claim: Wage inflation and real incomes are the main source of persistent inflation, so a stalling decline in wage growth is the indicator to watch.
claims.indicator: wage inflation figures, real income growth
claims.direction: inflation stays elevated if wage growth stops falling
claims.testable: yes: wage growth as inflation predictor

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: real income growth didn't keep up with the surge of inflation
claims.claim: The affordability problem (real income lagging the price level) cannot be fixed by lower prices (deflationary spiral) so the political resolution needs nominal income growth, which is inflationary.
claims.direction: nominal GDP and wages up

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: Once you've gone through that process, then it's easier the next time to see the price increases.
claims.claim: After a long period of too little inflation in which firms feared adjusting prices, one inflation episode teaches firms that they can raise prices, so price adjustment is easier and inflation more persistent and less stable.
claims.direction: inflation more persistent

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: income is is a more attractive source of use of fixed income in portfolios than diversification
claims.claim: With positive real yields and weaker diversification, investors use fixed income more for income than as a diversifier, opening room for alternative diversifiers.
claims.direction: fixed income used for income; alternatives take diversification role

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: negative stock bond correlation with high not great but at least for a while there positive real yields
claims.claim: Disinflation in the 1990s-2000s gave negative stock-bond correlation plus positive real yields, the golden period for 60/40 and risk parity.
claims.direction: bonds hedged equity

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: thinking about bonds as total return in the after in the in an environment of secular declining interest rates that's a pretty good strategy
claims.claim: Total-return bond investing worked because yields were in secular decline; at the zero bound that diversification argument reached its limit.
claims.direction: long bonds up in secular decline, limited at zero rates
claims.conditions: Secular falling yields; fails near zero lower bound
claims.testable: yes: bond returns by rate regime

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: opening the door if you will for other types of diversifying strategies to help fill the gap that is being created by the structural change
claims.claim: Weaker bond diversification opens space for systematic trend and liquid alternatives as diversifiers.
claims.direction: allocate to trend and liquid alternatives
claims.conditions: When stock-bond correlation is less negative

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: not only did we create inflation, we also created a tremendous amount of government debt along the way
claims.claim: Post-Covid inflation plus accelerated government debt creates fiscal dominance and financial-repression tail risk for fixed income.
claims.direction: long government bonds at risk

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: uncertainty sort of undid the secular decline in in in term premium and and uh real interest rates falling
claims.claim: Inflation uncertainty reversed the long decline in term premium and real rates.
claims.direction: term premium and real rates up

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: if prices are not free to be set by those signals, then you you got to recognize that.
claims.claim: Systematic models built on fundamentals assume free price setting; under financial repression or Fed-Treasury coordination rates are set administratively, so models must account for it (e.g. 1942-51 pegged rates).
claims.testable: partly: regime break in rates models

correction.issue: The '1942-51' date is not in the transcript. Rosenberg only refers to the pre-1951 Treasury-Fed accord regime (front end about 3/8%, long end about 2.5%, which he says someone should fact check).
correction.fix: Models built on fundamentals assume prices are free; under financial repression or Fed-Treasury coordination rates are set administratively, as in the US regime before the 1951 accord (fixed rates, long end about 2.5% per the speaker's uncertain recollection).

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: there are soft forms of repression that you need to be aware of
claims.claim: Models should not rely only on growth and inflation indicators to explain interest rates because soft financial repression can set them.

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: if you saw things like poor valuations in long-term government bonds, you might pivot away
claims.claim: As a fiduciary, systematic managers can avoid repression by moving away from long government bonds when valuations are poor, since repression transfers wealth from investors.
claims.direction: underweight long government bonds
claims.conditions: When valuation poor and repression likely

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: the different sources of returns have very different risk profiles
claims.claim: Separate beta, smart beta/risk premia and alpha explicitly because they need different data, skill and fee levels; market-neutral alpha is the hardest.

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: It is the hardest thing in our investing world to achieve market
claims.claim: Market-beta-and-factor-neutral alpha measured by information ratio is the hardest return stream to deliver.

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: we call it engineering for outcomes
claims.claim: Systematic funds are engineered to deliver a known return profile; trend has a specific profile that a well risk-budgeted implementation delivers, though not in all environments.

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: there are not all environments in which trend is a great strategy
claims.claim: Trend is not good in all environments but is very diversifying in particular ones, so it should be held for diversification.
claims.direction: trend good in crisis and strong markets
claims.conditions: Fails in trendless or reversal markets

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: trend on a broader context is is momentum a a and price momentum if
claims.claim: Trend is the time-series cousin of price momentum, the equity factor literature's big factor, so trend, factor and ML approaches blend.

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: trend hates reversals and and and and the policy uncertainty of this world has been you know a reversal engine
claims.claim: 2025 policy uncertainty created repeated reversals (inception 13 March 2025), which was very hard for trend; slower signals, multiple windows and breadth helped.
claims.direction: trend loses in reversals
claims.testable: yes: trend returns vs policy-uncertainty index

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: the law of active management information ratio is is skill times the square root of breath times transfer coefficient
claims.claim: Fundamental law: IR = skill x sqrt(breadth) x transfer coefficient; momentum has little skill so breadth and risk budgeting drive results.
claims.direction: more markets raises IR
claims.testable: yes: IR vs number of markets

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: The the key is breadth uh and then transfer coefficient like getting into your portfolios, managing the risk and and risk budgeting.
claims.claim: Use the law of active management: with weak per-bet skill, win through breadth and transfer coefficient.

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: how much breadth can you have is is sort of limited by by the structure because you need it to be able to scale
claims.claim: ETF structure caps breadth since the fund must scale, producing a trade-off between breadth, diversification and capacity.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it was just basically because of fortuitous selection of a few markets
claims.claim: Narrow replicator trend ETFs may have outperformed by lucky market selection rather than by systematic edge; commodities add breadth.
claims.testable: yes: compare narrow vs broad basket

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: the differentiator was did you have cocoa futures in your in your basket and the ones that did did great and the ones that didn't were underperformers
claims.claim: In 2024 trend funds were differentiated by whether they held cocoa futures, a small non-scalable contract, so BlackRock excluded it for scalability.

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: We're about somewhere about over 40 uh individual contracts
claims.claim: Their trend ETF trades about 40+ liquid contracts across FX, rates, commodities and equities, chosen by testing lists for liquidity, diversification and capacity.

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: own these things from a portfolio diversification perspective and less from a timing perspective
claims.claim: It is hard to forecast which environment (tails or middle) is next, so hold trend for diversification not for timing.

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: Credit is very capacity constrained on the short side.
claims.claim: Because credit shorts are capacity constrained, credit insights (Merton) were used to trade equities long-short instead.

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: how can we take signals and inputs from the equity to value uh the debt
claims.claim: Merton-style capital-structure signals link equity and debt value.
claims.indicator: Merton distance to default type signals

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: oh, what does debt do? It accelerates dispersion.
claims.claim: Limiting a market-neutral equity universe to ~500-600 firms with debt increases dispersion between winners and losers, especially in down markets, so alpha is stronger when diversification is needed.
claims.direction: long/short debt-bearing firms
claims.conditions: Defensive alpha strategy, market, beta and factor neutral
claims.testable: yes: dispersion in debt vs non-debt firms

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: When things are really tough, you batten down the hatches.
claims.claim: In down markets analysts focus on balance sheet, liquidity and credit access rather than the income statement, so overweighting balance-sheet signals gives alpha concentrated in drawdowns.
claims.indicator: balance sheet, liquidity, cost of credit signals
claims.testable: yes: signal IC by market state

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: that profile kind of looks like a short sorry long put option profile but without the timing and without the directionality
claims.claim: Defensive alpha is strong in very down markets and okay in up markets (long-put-like payoff) while being beta-neutral.

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: Trend has a particular the CTA smile. It's good in really down markets. It's good in really strong up markets.
claims.claim: Trend has a smile and defensive alpha a different convex shape; combine uncorrelated payoff profiles.

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: in systematic multi strategy we do it with a fixed income anchoring
claims.claim: Their multi-strategy blends uncorrelated profiles with fixed-income-like volatility as a bond complement, while the ETF version is a higher-octane equity substitute.

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: We we we call it implementation alpha.
claims.claim: Implementation alpha is larger in less liquid asset classes (credit, EM, high yield, commodities); in liquid ones execution is about scale and avoiding market impact.

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: they all get traded together
claims.claim: Internal crossing of index, active and systematic flows reduces market impact and a systematic investor's footprint.

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: Uh ETFs are a 40act rapper, but they just add some additional uh constraints
claims.claim: ETF wrappers constrain liquidity, capacity and leverage versus Cayman hedge fund vehicles; so quant strategies must be adapted.

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: leverage in an uncorrelated asset world means something very different than what leverage means in the beta world
claims.claim: Leverage limits designed for beta exposure misfit long-short neutral strategies.

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: attract a huge amount of notional leverage to to you know deliver a similar level of risk
claims.claim: Low-volatility contracts need huge notional per unit of risk, so contract choice weighs risk per notional too.
claims.direction: exclude low-vol contracts in capped-leverage wrappers

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: they're going to move to a total portfolio approach where each investment actually has to be justified in terms of its contribution to the total portfolio
claims.claim: CalPERS moving to a total portfolio approach mid-2026 should raise allocations to uncorrelated strategies.
claims.direction: more allocation to uncorrelated strategies

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: 40% of the S&P 500 market cap is now in the top 10 names
claims.claim: Record market-cap concentration (top 10 about 40% of S&P 500, tech and AI) makes market beta less diversified, increasing demand for uncorrelated liquid alternatives.

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: an uncorrelated return stream uh is very attractive in an environment where you've got a lot of concentration in your market betas
claims.claim: Uncorrelated return streams matter more than crisis alpha alone in concentrated markets.

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: 50 30 20 is the new 6040 like 20% of your portfolio in alternatives
claims.claim: Rule of thumb: 50/30/20 with 20% alternatives replaces 60/40.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: are we 95 or 99? You know, this rally could go on for quite a while
claims.claim: Allocators want to participate in the equity rally but with protection, via multi-strat, defensive alpha or trend.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: equally uh uncomfortable uh with the strategy when uh things are not trending so to speak
claims.claim: Institutions understand trend better but still doubt it when markets do not trend, as in 2025.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: I worry that that will come back to haunt the industry because at some point something is going to happen
claims.claim: Cheap trend ETFs (85 bps) compromise market breadth for scalability and may fail to match traditional CTA performance in a stress event.
claims.testable: partly: compare replicator to CTA indices

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: In the uncorrelated space there's much much more diversification.
claims.claim: In the uncorrelated space dispersion between products is large, so manager selection requires looking under the hood.

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: Most of that inflation concern is really in the US. Outside the US, you don't really see the same, you know, sort of factors that might contribute to resurgent inflation
claims.claim: The persistent-inflation concern is concentrated in the US; outside the US the factors that could drive resurgent inflation are not present, so the weakened stock-bond diversification story is mainly a US one.
claims.direction: inflation risk and weaker bond diversification mainly US
claims.conditions: US fiscal stimulus and wage pressure
claims.testable: yes - compare stock-bond correlation across regions

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: we used to have very stable inflation people could plan but postco I think going forward we'll continue to have kind of uh unstable inflation
claims.claim: Beyond a higher level, post-Covid inflation is likely to be less stable, which makes planning harder and keeps inflation uncertainty (and the term premium) elevated.
claims.direction: higher inflation uncertainty, higher term premium
claims.testable: yes - rolling inflation volatility vs term premium

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: how do you have edge and systematically put edge into portfolios and that's the kind of fundamental basis for for for our entire investment platform
claims.claim: BlackRock Systematic's platform rests on Grinold and Kahn's active portfolio management: find an edge and put it into portfolios systematically (the framework behind the fundamental law).
claims.testable: yes - IR decomposed into skill, breadth, transfer coefficient

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: we've been doing artificial intelligence before artificial intelligence was cool
claims.claim: Systematic firms have long used predictive AI (older machine learning) and now also generative AI; client demand now centers on generative AI, so the label hides which kind of model is doing the work.

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: there's this risk here that everybody's becoming systematic and then like nobody's systematic and we're losing the differentiation
claims.claim: If every manager becomes 'systematic' the label stops differentiating and edge gets crowded; he nevertheless sees it as good for the industry because systematic investing brings outcome orientation and explicit separation of return sources.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it was never popular. It was never uh a strategy talked much about or embraced much about uh embraced by by the very large asset managers frankly but that's changing
claims.claim: Pure trend following was historically ignored by the very large asset managers, but big houses (BlackRock, Fidelity, Invesco) have launched trend products in the last year or two, a structural shift in who offers trend and in what wrapper.
claims.indicator: launches of trend products by large managers
claims.direction: more trend capacity from large managers
claims.testable: partly - launch counts and AUM are observable

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: just taking a very simple strategy and and and keeping it simple and and replicating what investors expect out of trend and trying to deliver a trend-like experience
claims.claim: The pure trend ETF (ISMF) deliberately keeps a simple, expected trend profile, while the multi-strategy ETF (iAlt) is more ambitious and adds momentum and machine-learning elements to modify the payoff profile.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: delivering a return stream that's uncorrelated to equities over the kind of long term, but also delivering crisis alpha or whatever you like to call it at times of stress
claims.claim: Managed futures has a dual mandate, long-run return uncorrelated to equities and crisis alpha at times of stress, and the balance between them shapes signal speed and risk allocation across markets.
claims.direction: faster systems for crisis alpha, slower for long-run return
claims.testable: yes - speed-bucket backtest vs crisis-period returns

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: these very concentrated strategies, yeah, you're going to get some outperformance when when you're in the lucky right spot and then you're going to you're going to miss it in other days
claims.claim: Very concentrated trend baskets outperform when they happen to hold the right markets and miss other periods; the goal is consistency of delivering the intended outcome, not luck-driven outperformance.
claims.direction: broad baskets give more consistent results
claims.conditions: applies to ETFs limited by capacity
claims.testable: yes - dispersion of narrow vs broad trend baskets

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: because we'll have different types of equity drawdowns like you know short sharp ones more prolonged
claims.claim: Combining several defensive strategies is motivated by different equity-drawdown types (short sharp sell-offs versus prolonged ones like 2022 or the dot-com unwind), since each strategy protects in a different kind of drawdown.
claims.direction: diversify defensive strategies across drawdown types
claims.testable: yes - strategy returns by drawdown type

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: they saw a massive growth two threefold from the $5 trillion we see right now
claims.claim: A Capgemini report (as recalled by the host, number not exact) sees alternative investments growing two to three times from about $5 trillion, one data point for rising allocator demand for alternatives.
claims.direction: alternatives assets rise
claims.conditions: source and exact figure not verified in the talk

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: bringing this whole portfolio perspective to a broader audience to a retail audience moving away from kind of a a specific product focus uh evaluating products in isolation as opposed to evaluating in in in the context
claims.claim: The shift to a whole-portfolio (total portfolio) lens, long used by institutions, is spreading to retail: products should be judged by their contribution in context, not in isolation, which favors uncorrelated strategies.
claims.direction: more allocation to diversifying strategies

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: Trend is an alternative strategy. It invests somewhat in alternative assets
claims.claim: Liquid alternatives should be defined by strategy (long/short, momentum or trend as intellectual property) rather than by asset type; trend is an alternative strategy that can deliver uncorrelated return even when trading ordinary assets.

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: really get you away from that market beta enough. And this is where allocating a good portion of your portfolio
claims.claim: Small tilts around a concentrated market beta do not diversify enough; the answer is allocating a sizeable portion (the 20% of 50/30/20) to uncorrelated strategies.
claims.direction: raise alternatives to around 20%
claims.testable: yes - portfolio simulation of tilt vs allocation size

claims.speaker: Jeff Rosenberg
claims.quote: it may be a mixture between taking some ill liquidity premium for diversification um in terms of marktomarket risk liquid alternatives for diversification
claims.claim: The 20% alternatives sleeve can mix illiquid assets (earning an illiquidity premium and showing smoother marks) with liquid alternatives (true diversification, daily marks); his own preference is all liquid.
claims.direction: mix of illiquid and liquid alternatives
claims.testable: partly - premium net of smoothing is debated

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: bond equity correlation shift is a big driver for for allocators
claims.claim: From the allocator side, the shift in bond-equity correlation is a main driver of the case for hedge fund strategies, liquid alternatives and trend.
claims.direction: more allocations to alternatives as correlation turns positive

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the fees are so low that you need 10 billion to make it even a a a good business
claims.claim: At ~85 bps flat fees an ETF needs about $10 billion to be a viable business, pushing sponsors to cut breadth for scalability (against full-fee CTAs at ~115 bps), which is the mechanism behind the narrow-basket risk.
claims.direction: narrower baskets in low-fee trend ETFs
claims.testable: yes - fee, AUM and breadth of trend ETFs
